schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE A (A1 INT, A2 INT);
CREATE TABLE B (B1 INT, B2 INT);
q1: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A AS X, B AS Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B AS X, A AS Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A AS X, B AS Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B AS X, A AS Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
counterexample: INSERT INTO A (A1, A2) VALUES (1, 10), (2, 20); INSERT INTO B (B1, B2) VALUES (1, 100), (3, 300);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because they join tables A and B on different conditions. Q1 joins A and B where A.A1 = B.B1, while Q2 joins A and B where B.A1 = A.B1. This difference in join conditions can lead to different sets of results.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have at least one row in A where A1 = B1 and another row in A where A1 != B1. The presence of such rows will cause Q1 and Q2 to return different results.
q1_validation_sql: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A AS X, B AS Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2_validation_sql: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B AS X, A AS Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
